Costly Devotion
KOST-lee dee-VOH-shun
noun phrase (Mark 14; the alabaster box)
From the account of Mary's breaking the alabaster box of precious ointment upon Christ; the principle that true worship offers to God what truly costs.

📖 Biblical Definition

Costly devotion is the principle, displayed when Mary broke the alabaster box of very precious spikenard upon the Lord, that true worship and love give to God what truly costs the giver. As Jesus sat at meat in Bethany, a woman came with an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious, broke the box, and poured it on His head; the worth of it was three hundred pence, near a labourer's year of wages. Some present murmured that it was waste, but the Lord rebuked them: “Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me… She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.” He set her deed in everlasting honour, that wheresoever the gospel should be preached, this should be told for a memorial of her. The dictionary binds her act to David's confession when he refused to offer to the LORD that which cost him nothing: “I will surely buy it of thee at a price.” Costly devotion is the opposite of the cheap religion that offers God leftovers, spare moments, and what costs no sacrifice. It is not extravagance for its own sake, nor the buying of merit, for salvation is free; it is the overflow of a heart that has received much and counts no offering too precious for the Lord who gave Himself. The dictionary marks it against both the utilitarian spirit that calls all such offering “waste,” and against the false notion that God can be served acceptably by what costs us nothing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The principle, shown in Mary's breaking the alabaster box upon Christ (Mark 14:3-8), that true worship offers God what truly costs; against both the utilitarian who calls it waste and the cheap religion that gives God leftovers.

expand to see more

COSTLY DEVOTION, noun phrase. The giving to God of what truly costs the worshipper, in love and worship.

Mary broke an alabaster box of very precious spikenard and poured it on Christ (Mark 14:3).

Some called it waste; the Lord called it a good work and set it in everlasting memorial.

David refused to offer that which cost him nothing (2 Samuel 24:24).

Not the buying of merit, but the overflow of a heart that has received much.

📖 Key Scripture

Mr 14:3 — "And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head."

Mr 14:6 — "And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me."

Mr 14:8 — "She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying."

2 Sa 24:24 — "And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The utilitarian spirit dismisses costly worship as “waste,” while cheap religion offers God leftovers; both miss the heart that counts no offering too precious for the Lord who gave Himself.

expand to see more

The utilitarian objection—“this might have been sold and given to the poor”—sounds pious but was rebuked by the Lord Himself. The dictionary does not despise mercy to the poor, which Scripture everywhere commands; it names the corruption that measures every act of worship by its visible usefulness and calls extravagant love toward Christ a waste. Mary's deed was useful for nothing the world could count, yet the Lord called it a good work and gave it an everlasting memorial. There is a devotion poured out on Christ that needs no further justification than that it was offered to Him.

The opposite and commoner corruption is the cheap religion that offers God only what costs nothing—the spare hour, the loose change, the half-hearted service, the worship that demands no sacrifice. David refused to bring the LORD an offering that cost him nothing, and Mary broke a year's wages over the head of her Lord. The dictionary recovers costly devotion not as a buying of merit—salvation is wholly free—but as the natural overflow of a heart that has received the unspeakable gift and therefore counts nothing too precious to pour out on the Giver.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the account of the alabaster box (Greek alabastron) of spikenard (nardos pistike); the deed is “a good work” (kalon ergon) the Lord commends, bound to David's refusal to offer what costs nothing.

expand to see more

Alabastron, Greek, a flask of alabaster, here broken to pour out its whole contents.

Nardos pistike, Greek, pure or genuine spikenard, a costly aromatic ointment.

Three hundred pence (denaria) was near a year's wages for a labourer.

Kalon ergon, Greek, “a good work,” the Lord's verdict on the deed (Mark 14:6).

David's “that which doth cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24) sets the principle in the law of offering.

Usage

"The pastor preached the alabaster box to rebuke a religion that gives God leftovers and spare moments."

"He recalled David's refusal to offer what cost nothing, and gave his best to the Lord and not his remnants."

"She poured out her costly years on Christ, and counted as gain what the world called waste."
